snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ TNPSC Unit 9 Hook: 69%: TN. 76th Amend: 9th Sch. Sattanathan: 1970. 1st Amend: 1951. MBC: 20%. SC: 18%.

quick_notes.title: Evolution of Reservation
quick_notes.detail: Communal G.O. (1921). After Champakam Dorairajan case (1951), 1st Constitutional Amendment added Art 15(4) to allow reservation.
quick_notes.explanation: The Communal Government Order of 1921 was a rule in the Madras Presidency that reserved a share of government jobs for different communities based on their population. In the Champakam Dorairajan case of 1951, the Supreme Court ruled that such reservations violated the right to equality because the Constitution did not initially allow them. To fix this, the First Constitutional Amendment added Article 15, clause 4, which allows the state to make special arrangements for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes, as well as for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, thereby making reservations constitutional.

quick_notes.title: Reservation Commissions
quick_notes.explanation: Reservation Commissions are groups formed by the government to study and recommend how to fairly distribute benefits like government jobs and education seats for Backward Classes, which are groups of people who are socially and educationally behind others. The first Backward Classes Commission was chaired by Sattanathan in 1970, so it is called the Sattanathan Commission; it was the first commission to specifically study Backward Classes in India. The second commission was led by Ambasankar in 1982, known as the Ambasankar Commission, which updated the list of communities needing help. The third important commission was the Janarthanam Commission, which focused on sub-categorizing Backward Classes, meaning it divided them into smaller groups to ensure the most needy communities got more benefits. These commissions all submitted reports to the government, which then used their findings to create laws and policies for reservations, which are the set-aside quotas for these groups.

quick_notes.title: The 69% Model
quick_notes.detail: Current breakup: BC (30%), MBC (20%), SC (18%), ST (1%). MBC includes DNT.
quick_notes.explanation: TITLE: The 69% Model In Tamil Nadu, the government reserves a certain percentage of seats in education and government jobs for people from specific communities to help them overcome historical disadvantages. This reservation system is called the 69% Model because it reserves a total of 69% of seats for these communities. The reservation is broken down into four main categories: Backward Classes (BC) get 30%, Most Backward Classes (MBC) get 20%, Scheduled Castes (SC) get 18%, and Scheduled Tribes (ST) get 1%. The MBC category includes a group called Denotified Tribes (DNT), which refers to communities that were once classified as "criminal tribes" under British rule but are now officially recognized as backward. This model is based on the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Reservation of Seats in Educational Institutions and of Appointments or Posts in the Services under the State) Act, 1993, which is protected under the Ninth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, meaning it cannot be challenged in court for violating Fundamental Rights. The total reservation adds up to 69%, which is higher than the 50% limit set by the Supreme Court, but Tamil Nadu continues to follow this model under a special constitutional provision.

quick_notes.title: 76th Constitutional Amendment
quick_notes.detail: Passed in 1994 (under J. Jayalalithaa) to place TN's 69% reservation in the 9th Schedule (beyond judicial review).
quick_notes.explanation: The 76th Constitutional Amendment was passed in 1994 when J. Jayalalithaa was the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu. This amendment added a Tamil Nadu law that gives 69% reservation in government jobs and college admissions to the Ninth Schedule of the Indian Constitution. quick_notes.title: Social Harmony
quick_notes.detail: Tamil Nadu ranks high in social development due to the Inclusive Growth model and pluralistic culture.
quick_notes.explanation: Social Harmony means different groups of people living together peacefully and with mutual respect. Inclusive Growth is an economic model that ensures the benefits of development reach all sections of society, including the poor and marginalized, not just the wealthy. Pluralistic Culture refers to a society where many different religions, languages, and traditions are accepted and celebrated equally. Tamil Nadu has achieved high social development, meaning better education, health, and living standards for its people, because it follows Inclusive Growth and has a long history of Pluralistic Culture. This approach helps reduce inequality and conflict, allowing everyone to participate in the state's progress.
